catalog_quote: Takanan languages have complex and still poorly understood accentual systems. The function of these systems is to delimit the phonological/prosodic word; none of them are lexically/morphologically constrastive. ... In the stress systems that have been studied to some degree (i.e., Ese Ejja, Araona and Tacana), stress falls on one of the first three syllables or morae counting from the left. Which syllable/mora receives stress (1st, 2nd or 3rd) depends on a range of different phonological and morphological factors which differ according to the languages. In Tacana, the basic rule is that, underlyingly, most lexemes are stressed on the 3rd mora (vowel or semi-vowel y [j]) from the left. This pattern is revealed on the surface when the prosodic word contains at least four morae, as in (3). sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are one work: Van Wynen & Van Wynen 1962 'Fonemas tacana y modelos de acentuación' (Notas Lingüísticas de Bolivia 6, 32 pp., Spanish translation by Liendo Lazarte; Glottolog 131222 and 688467 duplicate it), the only dedicated Tacana stress analysis and the source Guillaume cites for the catalog rule. No open copy of the full booklet exists: the Rosetta Project extracts on archive. 8-16, 22-23) and the word list (pp. 30-32); section 6 'Modelos de acentuación' is missing; SIL archive 10799 says 'Not Available Online'; Google Books shows only citing works; HathiTrust/WorldCat blocked; Harvard holds a print copy (scan-and-deliver eligible). What was read is consistent with the catalog: the stress pattern is keyed to syllable count with vowel sequences as single syllables, and the three stress-marked forms (eaṣéaṣeni, aṣeáṣetaitia, miméa) fall where Guillaume's 3rd-mora/penult rule predicts; but no rule statement was obtained, so the catalog's deciding source (Guillaume 2023/HAL v2 pp. 8-9, re-read and unchanged; Guillaume 2024 fn. 5 adds [w] as a mora) stands. Acquiring section 6 is high priority because Van Wynen's 'according to the number of syllables' phrasing may show a syllable-counting rather than mora-counting analysis, which bears on the weight-hedged coding. updated in our files.

new_statements.translation: The stress pattern according to the number of syllables (see section 6) corroborates this interpretation. ... When the low vowels /e/ and /a/ occur together across a morpheme boundary but inside the word, they are interpreted as two distinct syllables and the accent can fall on either of the vowels: [eaṣéaṣeni] 'I am hunting'; [aṣeáṣetaitia] 'I have hunted'.

new_statements.reading: First-hand primary source (SIL fieldwork 1956-61), but not a rule statement: the rule itself sits in the unheld section 6. What is read says stress position is a function of syllable count (with vowel sequences /ia ai ua au ie ei ue eu iu ui/ counted as single syllables), and the stress-marked forms — eaṣéaṣeni and aṣeáṣetaitia stressed on the 3rd vowel from the left, miméa (p. 13) on the penult of a 3-vowel word — all agree with the catalog's Guillaume rule (3rd mora from the left in words of ≥4 morae, penultimate otherwise). The 'según el número de las sílabas' wording leaves open whether Van Wynen's own analysis counted syllables rather than morae, the very point behind the weight-hedged coding.

new_statements.relation_note: Against catalog_records (Gordon: penultimate stress = penult at every length): the marked six-syllable forms are stressed on the third syllable from the left, i.e. the antepenult-minus-one, so the fixed: penultimate syllable coding fails at n>=4 syllables, exactly as the site's editor's review already states ('the standing census coding (penult at every length 2-8) is wrong at n>=5 regardless'). Against existing_statements: this is the same passage the earlier reader quoted; my re-reading and the page-image check agree with it. Against the site's Guillaume 2023 rule (3rd mora from the left when >=4 morae, else penult): agrees in every marked form.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The held pages state only that stress position is a function of the syllable count (the rule itself is in the unheld section 6), with vowel sequences ia ai ua au ie ei ue eu iu ui counted as single syllables and e+a across morphemes counted as two. The stress-marked forms (verified on the page images) put the accent on the third syllable from the left in the six-syllable words e.a.ṣé.a.ṣe.ni and a.ṣe.á.ṣe.tai.tia (fourth from the right, so not penult) and on the penult of the three-syllable mi.mé.a; that is the same distribution as the third-mora-from-the-left / penult-below-four-morae rule in Guillaume 2023 (which cites this booklet). Whether Van Wynen counted syllables or morae is left open by the held pages.
new_statements.exceptions: e+a across morphemes: 'el acento puede caer sobre cualquier de las vocales' (either vowel can bear stress); miméa is the one morpheme-internal e+a sequence, treated as two syllables; p. 14 notes that in younger speakers the group /ea/ is replaced by /ia/ (eáwi -> iáwi 'agua'), which changes the syllable count.
new_statements.identity_note: Van Wynen & Van Wynen 1962 describe the Tacana of Ixiamas, Tumupasa and San Buenaventura (NW Bolivia) from 1956-61 fieldwork and note an age difference (older speakers keep /ea/ where younger ones say /ia/, p. 14). Guillaume's data are from 2009-2013 fieldwork on the same language. The wrong item at SIL 11879 is a Cuicatec (cux) alphabet leaflet, not a Tacana variety.

readall_conflicts: The catalog record of record (Gordon, via StressTyp2's reading of Key 1968:29) codes fixed penultimate stress at every length. Every primary source that could be opened contradicts that at four or more morae: Van Wynen & Van Wynen 1962 (pp. 12-13, stress marks verified on the page image) stress eaṣéaṣeni and aṣeáṣetaitia on the third syllable from the left, and Guillaume 2023 (held by the project in the same check folder, p. 8, not in the works list) states the rule as 'stressed on the syllable that contains the third mora (vowel or semi-vowel y [j])' when the prosodic word has at least four morae, penultimate otherwise, citing Van Wynen 1962 and his own 2009-2013 fieldnotes. Even Key's own wording, as quoted by StressTyp2 on the site record (not verified against the book, which is not online), restricts penult to 'words without affixes spoken in isolation' and gives second-syllable, third-syllable and mixed classes for affixed words, so the disagreement is between Gordon's single-position coding and the sources rather than between the sources themselves. The residual open point is syllables versus morae: Van Wynen's held pages speak of 'el número de las sílabas' but contain no stress-marked example in which a bimoraic VV syllable precedes the stress, so they cannot decide between his syllable count and Guillaume's mora count; Guillaume's yawíkwaṣe (VV.CV́.CV.CV) is the deciding form and comes from his own data.

sources.quote: Primary stress is generally on the penult of words without affixes spoken in isolation. When affixes are added new stress patterns occur. From these patterns Tacana words can be classified into three classes:1. stress on the second syllable2. stress on the third syllable3. mixed. (Key 1968:29)
